## ARGUMENT

### I. Removal on improper-joinder grounds requires the removing party to show there is no reasonable basis to predict that Plaintiff might recover against the in-state defendant.

Federal courts are courts of limited jurisdiction, and the party invoking removal bears the burden of establishing that federal jurisdiction exists and that removal was proper. *Manguno v. Prudential Prop. & Cas. Ins. Co.*, 276 F.3d 720, 723 (5th Cir. 2002); *Gasch v. Hartford Accident & Indem. Co.*, 491 F.3d 278, 281–82 (5th Cir. 2007). Because removal raises significant federalism concerns, the removal statute is strictly construed, and any doubt is resolved in favor of remand. *Gasch*, 491 F.3d at 281–82; *Great Plains Tr. Co. v. Morgan Stanley Dean Witter & Co.*, 313 F.3d 305, 312–13 (5th Cir. 2002).

The improper-joinder doctrine is a narrow exception to the rule that a properly joined, non-diverse defendant defeats diversity jurisdiction. *Smallwood v. Ill. Cent. R.R. Co.*, 385 F.3d 568, 573 (5th Cir. 2004) (en banc). Absent actual fraud in the pleading of jurisdictional facts, the removing party must demonstrate "that there is no possibility of recovery by the plaintiff against an in-state defendant, which stated differently means that there is no reasonable basis for the district court to predict that the plaintiff might be able to recover against an in-state defendant." *Id.*; accord *Flagg v. Stryker Corp.*, 819 F.3d 132, 136–37 (5th Cir. 2016) (en banc); *Mumfrey v. CVS Pharmacy, Inc.*, 719 F.3d 392, 401 (5th Cir. 2013). This Court has repeatedly described that burden as a heavy one. *Griggs v. State Farm Lloyds*, 181 F.3d 694, 699 (5th Cir. 1999); *Travis v. Irby*, 326 F.3d 644, 649 (5th Cir. 2003); *McDonal v. Abbott Labs.*, 408 F.3d 177, 183 (5th Cir. 2005).

The standard is framed in terms of whether a reasonable basis for recovery exists, and it is the removing party that must negate that basis. The plaintiff need not prove that she will prevail, or even that she is likely to. The question is whether there is a reasonable possibility of recovery, as opposed to one that is merely theoretical. *Campbell v. Stone Ins., Inc.*, 509 F.3d 665, 669 (5th Cir. 2007); *Travis*, 326 F.3d at 648. A defendant who shows only that the plaintiff's claim is weak, novel, or likely to fail on the merits has not carried that burden.

### II. The court's inquiry is confined, and every doubt is resolved in the plaintiff's favor.

To decide whether the removing party has met its burden, the court ordinarily conducts a Rule 12(b)(6)-type analysis, asking whether the complaint states a claim against the in-state defendant under state law. *Smallwood*, 385 F.3d at 573; *Int'l Energy Ventures Mgmt., L.L.C. v. United Energy Grp., Ltd.*, 818 F.3d 193, 200–08 (5th Cir. 2016) (applying the federal pleading standard to that inquiry). Only in the rare case where the plaintiff has "misstated or omitted discrete facts that would determine the propriety of joinder" may the court pierce the pleadings. *Smallwood*, 385 F.3d at 573–74. Even then, the inquiry is summary and may not become a pretrial trial on the merits. *Id.* at 574; *Davidson v. Ga.-Pac., L.L.C.*, 819 F.3d 758, 765 (5th Cir. 2016).

In conducting this review, the court must evaluate all factual allegations in the light most favorable to the plaintiff. It must also resolve all contested issues of fact and all ambiguities in controlling state law in the plaintiff's favor. *Guillory v. PPG Indus., Inc.*, 434 F.3d 303, 308 (5th Cir. 2005); *Cuevas v. BAC Home Loans Servicing, LP*, 648 F.3d 242, 249 (5th Cir. 2011). It follows that where state law is unsettled, or where the complaint pleads facts supporting a plausible claim against the non-diverse defendant, the removing party has not shown that there is no reasonable basis for recovery, and remand is required.

### III. Application

Defendants, as the removing parties, must establish that Plaintiff has no reasonable basis for recovery against the in-state defendant. For the reasons above, they must make that showing on the face of the Complaint, read in Plaintiff's favor and under the governing state-law standard. If they cannot, the in-state defendant was properly joined, complete diversity is lacking, and the case must be remanded.
